div.stage: SCENE: —The Orchestra represents a public square in Athens; in the background are two houses with an alley between them.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.stage: Swinging the lantern, which is to be a signal for the other women; in high tragic style.
sp.p: Oh! Thou shining light of my earthenware lamp, from this high spot shalt thou look abroad. Oh! lamp, I will tell thee thine origin and thy future; 'tis the rapid whirl of the potter's wheel that has lent thee thy shape, and thy wick counterfeits the glory of the sun; mayst thou send the agreed signal flashing afar! In thee alone do we confide, and thou art worthy, for thou art near us when we practise the various postures in which Aphrodite delights upon our couches, and none dreams even in the midst of her sports of seeking to avoid thine eye that watches us. Thou alone shinest into the secret recesses of our thighs and dost singe the hair that groweth there, and with thy flame dost light the actions of our loves. If we open some cellar stored with fruits and wine, thou art our companion, and never dost thou betray or reveal to a neighbor the secrets thou hast learned about us. Therefore thou shalt know likewise the whole of the plot that I have planned with my friends, the women, at the festival of the Scirophoria. She pauses and looks about her.I see none of those I was expecting, though dawn approaches; the Assembly is about to gather and we must take our seats in spite of Phyromachus, who forsooth would say, “It is meet the women sit apart and hidden from the eyes of the men.” Why, have they not been able then to procure the false beards that they must wear, or to steal their husbands' cloaks? Ah! I see a light approaching; let us draw somewhat aside, for fear it should be a man.

div.stage: She hides in the alley. From the right a woman enters, followed almost immediately by others. All are carrying staffs, men's sandals, and cloaks over their arms.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Let us start, it is high time; as we left our dwellings, the cock was crowing for the second time.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: And I have spent the whole night waiting for you.She emerges from the alley.But come, let us call our neighbor by scratching at her door; and gently too, so that her husband may hear nothing.

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.stage: Coming out of her house; she is dressed like a man, with a staff in her hand.
sp.p: I was putting on my shoes, when I heard you scratching, for I was not asleep, so there! Oh! my dear, my husband (he is a Salaminian) never left me an instant's peace, but was at me, for ever at me, all night long, so that it was only just now that I was able to filch his cloak.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: I see Clinarete coming too, along with Sostrate and their next-door neighbor Philaenete.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.stage: To the women that are just arriving; in a loud voice.
sp.p: Hurry yourselves then, for Glyce has sworn that the last comer shall forfeit three measures of wine and a choenix of pease.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Don't you see Melistice, the wife of Smicythion, hurrying hither in her big shoes?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: I think she is the only one of us all who has had no trouble in getting rid of her husband.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: And can't you see Geusistrate, the tavern-keeper's wife, with a lamp in her hand?

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: And the wives of Philodoretus and Chaeretades, and a great many others; all the useful people in the city, in fact.

sp.speaker: Third Woman
sp.p: Oh! my dear, I have had such trouble in getting away! My husband ate such a surfeit of sprats last evening that he was coughing and choking the whole night long.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Take your seats, and, since you are all gathered here at last, let us see if what we decided on at the feast of the Scirophoria has been duly done.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Yes. Firstly, as agreed, I have let the hair under my armpits grow thicker than a bush; furthermore, whilst my husband was at the Assembly, I rubbed myself from head to foot with oil and then stood the whole day long in the sun.

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: So did I. I began by throwing away my razor, so that I might get quite hairy, and no longer resemble a woman.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Have you the beards that we had all to get ourselves for the Assembly?

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Yea, by Hecate! Is this not a fine one?

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: Aye, much finer even than the one Epicrates has.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: And you?

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Yes, yes; look, they all nod assent.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: I see that you have got all the rest too, Spartan shoes, staffs and men's cloaks, as it was arranged.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: I have brought Lamias' club, which I stole from him while he slept.

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: What, the club that makes him fart with its weight?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: By Zeus the Deliverer, if he had the skin of Argus, he would know better than any other how to shepherd the popular herd. But come, let us finish what has yet to be done, while the stars are still shining; the Assembly, at which we mean to be present, will open at dawn.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Good; you must take up your place at the foot of the platform and facing the Prytanes.

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: I have brought this with me to card during the Assembly.

div.stage: She shows some wool.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: During the Assembly, wretched woman?

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: Surely, by Artemis! shall I hear any less well if I am doing a bit of carding? My little ones are all but naked.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Think of her wanting to card! whereas we must not let anyone see the smallest part of our bodies. 'Twould be a fine thing if one of us, in the midst of the discussion, rushed on to the speaker's platform and, flinging her cloak aside, showed her Phormisius. If, on the other hand, we are the first to take our seats closely muffled in our cloaks, none will know us. Let us fix these beards on our chins, so that they spread all over our bosoms. How can we fail then to be mistaken for men?

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Agyrrhius has deceived everyone, thanks to the beard of Pronomus; yet he was no better than a woman, and you see how he now holds the first position in the city.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Thus, I adjure you by this day that is about to dawn, let us dare to copy him and let us be clever enough to possess ourselves of the management of affairs. Let us save the ship of state, which just at present none seems able either to sail or row.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: But where shall we find orators in an Assembly of women?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Nothing simpler. Is it not said that the cleverest speakers are those who get made love to most often? Well, thanks to the gods, we are that by nature.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: There's no doubt of that; but the worst of it is our inexperience.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: That's the very reason we are gathered here, in order to prepare the speech we must make in the Assembly. Hasten, therefore, all you who know aught of speaking, to fix on your beards.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Oh! you stupid thing! is there ever a one among us cannot use her tongue?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Come, look sharp, on with your beard and become a man. As for me, I will do the same in case I should have a fancy for getting on to the platform. Here are the chaplets.

div.stage: They all put on their beards.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Oh! great gods! my dear Praxagora, do look here! Is it not laughable?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: How laughable?

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Our beards look like broiled cuttle-fishes.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Priest, bring in the cat. Step forward, please! Silence, Ariphrades! Go and take your seat. Now, who wishes to speak?

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: I do.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Then put on this chaplet and success be with you.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: There!

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Well then! begin.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Before drinking?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Hah! she wants to drink!

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Why, what else is the meaning of this chaplet?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Get you hence! you would probably have played us this trick also before the people.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Well! don't the men drink then in the Assembly?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Now she's telling us the men drink!

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Yes, by Artemis, and neat wine too. That's why their decrees breathe of drunkenness and madness. And why libations, why so many ceremonies, if wine plays no part in them? Besides, they abuse each other like drunken men, and you can see the archers dragging more than one uproarious drunkard out of the market-place.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Go back to your seat, you are wandering.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Ah! I should have done better not to have muffled myself in this beard; my throat's afire and I feel I shall die of thirst.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Who else wishes to speak?

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: I do.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Quick then, take the chaplet; the time's running short. Try to speak worthily, let your language be truly manly, and lean on your staff with dignity.

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: I had rather have seen one of your regular orators giving you wise advice; but, as that is not to be, it behoves me to break silence; I cannot, for my part indeed, allow the tavern-keepers to fill up their wine-pits with water. No, by the two goddesses—

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: What? By the two goddesses! Wretched woman, where are your senses?

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: Eh! what? ... I have not asked you for a drink.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: No, but you want to pass for a man, and you swear by the two goddesses. Otherwise you did very well.

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: Well then. By Apollo—

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Stop! All these details of language must be adjusted; else it is quite useless to go to the Assembly.

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: Give me back the chaplet; I wish to speak again, for I think I have got hold of something good. You women who are listening to me —

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Women again; why, you wretched creature, it's men that you are addressing.

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: That's the fault of Epigonus; I caught sight of him way over there, and I thought I was speaking to women.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Come, withdraw and remain seated in the future. I am going to take this chaplet myself and speak in your name. May the gods grant success to my plans! My country is as dear to me as it is to you, and I groan, I am grieved at all that is happening in it. Scarcely one in ten of those who rule it is honest, and all the others are bad. If you appoint fresh chiefs, they will do still worse. It is hard to correct your peevish humor; you fear those who love you and throw yourselves at the feet of those who betray you. There was a time when we had no assemblies, and then we all thought Agyrrhius a dishonest man; now they are established, he who gets money thinks everything is as it should be, and he who does not, declares all who sell their votes to be worthy of death.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: By Aphrodite, that is well spoken.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Why, wretched woman, you have actually called upon Aphrodite. Oh! what a fine thing it would have been if you had said that in the Assembly!

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: But I would not have done it then.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Well, mind you don't fall into the habit.Resuming the oratorical manner.When we were discussing the alliance, it seemed as though it were all over with Athens if it fell through. No sooner was it made than we were vexed and angry, and the orator who had caused its adoption was compelled to seek safety in flight. Is there talk of equipping a fleet? The poor man says, yes, but the rich citizen and the countryman say, no. You were angered against the Corinthians and they with you; now they are well disposed towards you, be so towards them. As a rule the Argives are dull, but the Argive Hieronymus is a distinguished chief. Herein lies a spark of hope; but Thrasybulus is far from Athens and you do not recall him.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Oh! what a brilliant man!

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: That's better! that's fitting applause.Continuing her speech.Citizens, you are the ones who are the cause of all this trouble. You vote yourselves salaries out of the public funds and care only for your own personal interests; hence the state limps along like Aesimus. But if you hearken to me, you will be saved. I assert that the direction of affairs must be handed over to the women, for they are the ones who have charge and look after our households.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Very good, very good, that's perfect!

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: Go on, go on.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: They are worth more than you are, as I shall prove. First of all they wash all their wool in warm water, according to the ancient practice; you will never see them changing their method. Ah! if Athens only acted thus, if it did not take delight in ceaseless innovations, would not its happiness be assured? Then the women sit down to cook, just as they always did; they carry things on their head just as they always did; they keep the Thesmophoria, just as they always did; they knead their cakes just as they always did; they make their husbands angry just as they always did; they receive their lovers in their houses just as they always did; they buy dainties just as they always did; they love unmixed wine just as they always did; they delight in being loved just as they always did. Let us therefore hand Athens over to them without endless discussions, without bothering ourselves about what they will do; let us simply hand them over the power, remembering that they are mothers and will therefore spare the blood of our soldiers; besides, who will know better than a mother how to forward provisions to the front? Woman is adept at getting money for herself and will not easily let herself be deceived; she understands deceit too well herself. I omit a thousand other advantages. Take my advice and you will live in perfect happiness.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: How beautiful this is, my dearest Praxagora, how clever! But where, pray, did you learn all these pretty things?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: When the countryfolk were seeking refuge in the city, I lived on the Pnyx with my husband, and there I learnt to speak through listening to the orators.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: Then, dear, it's not astonishing that you are so eloquent and clever; henceforward you shall be our leader, so put your great ideas into execution. But if Cephalus belches forth insults against you, what answer will you give him in the Assembly?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: I shall say that he is drivelling.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: But all the world knows that.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: I shall furthermore say that he is a raving madman.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: There's nobody who does not know that.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: That he, as excellent a statesman as he is, is a clumsy potter.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: And if the blear-eyed Neoclides comes to insult you?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: To him I shall say, “Go and look at a dog's arse.”

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: And if they fly at you?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Oh! I shall shake them off as best I can; never fear, I know how to use this tool.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: But there is one thing we don't think of. If the Scythians drag you away, what will you do?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: With my arms akimbo like this, I will never, never let myself be taken round the middle.

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: If they seize you, we will bid them let you go.

sp.speaker: First Woman
sp.p: That's the best way. But how are we going to remember to lift our arms in the Assembly when it's our legs we are used to lifting?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: It's difficult; yet it must be done, and the arm shown naked to the shoulder in order to vote. Quick now, put on these tunics and these Laconian shoes, as you see the men do each time they go to the Assembly or for a walk. When this is done, fix on your beards, and when they are arranged in the best way possible, dress yourselves in the cloaks you have stolen from your husbands; finally start off, leaning on your staffs and singing some old man's song as the villagers do.

sp.speaker: Second Woman
sp.p: Well spoken; and let us hurry to get to the Pnyx before the women from the country, for they will no doubt not fail to come there.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Quick, quick, for it's the custom that those who are not at the Pnyx early in the morning return home empty-handed.

div.stage: Praxagora and the First and Second Women depart; those who are left behind form the Chorus.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Move forward, citizens, move forward; let us not forget to give ourselves this name and may that of woman never slip out of our mouths; woe to us, if it were discovered that we had laid such a plot in the darkness of night.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Let us go to the Assembly then, fellow-citizens; for the Thesmothetes have declared that only those who arrive at daybreak with haggard eye and covered with dust, without having snatched time to eat anything but a snack of garlic-pickle, shall alone receive the triobolus. Walk up smartly, Charitimides, Smicythus and Draces, and do not fail in any point of your part; let us first demand our fee and then vote for all that may perchance be useful for our partisans. . . Ah! what am I saying? I meant to say, for our fellow-citizens.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Let us drive away these men of the city who used to stay at home and chatter round the table in the days when only an obolus was paid, whereas now one is stifled by the crowds at the Pnyx. No! during the archonship of generous Myronides, none would have dared to let himself be paid for the trouble he spent over public business; each one brought his own meal of bread, a couple of onions, three olives and some wine in a little wine-skin. But nowadays we run here to earn the three obols, for the citizen has become as mercenary as the stonemason.

sp.stage: The Chorus marches away. Blepyrus appears in the doorway of his house, wearing Praxagora's Persian sandals and saffron robe.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: What does this mean? My wife has vanished! it is nearly daybreak and she does not return! I had to take a crap! I woke up and hunted in the darkness for my shoes and my cloak; but grope where I would, I couldn't find them. Meanwhile Mr. O'Shit was already knocking on the door and I had only just time to seize my wife's little mantle and her Persian slippers. But where shall I find a place where I can take a crap? Bah! One place is as good as another at night-time; no one will see me. Ah! what a damned fool I was to take a wife at my age, and how I could thrash myself for having acted so stupidly! It's certainty she's not gone out for any honest purpose. But the thing to do now is to take a crap.

div.stage: He squats.

sp.speaker: A Man
sp.stage: Looking out of the window of the house next door.
sp.p: Who's that? Is that not my neighbor Blepyrus? Why, yes, it's no other. Tell me, what's all that yellow about you? Can it be Cinesias who has befouled you so?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: No, no, I only slipped on my wife's tunic to come out in.

sp.speaker: Man
sp.p: And where is your cloak?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: I cannot tell you; I hunted for it vainly on the bed.

sp.speaker: Man
sp.p: And why did you not ask your wife for it?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Ah! why indeed! because she is not in the house; she has run away, and I greatly fear that she may be doing me an ill turn.

sp.speaker: Man
sp.p: But, by Poseidon, it's the same with myself. My wife has disappeared with my cloak, and what is still worse, with my shoes as well; I cannot find them anywhere.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Nor can I my Laconian ones; but as I urgently needed to crap, I popped my feet into these slippers, so as not to soil my blanket, which is brand new.

sp.speaker: Man
sp.p: What does it mean? Can some friend have invited her to a feast?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: I expect so, for she does not generally misconduct herself, as far as I know.

sp.speaker: Man
sp.p: What are you doing, making well-ropes? Are you never going to be done? As for myself, I would like to go to the Assembly, and it is time to start, but I've got to find my cloak; I have only one.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: I am going to have a look too, when I have finished crapping; but I really think there must be a wild pear obstructing my rectum.

sp.speaker: Man
sp.p: Is it the one which Thrasybulus spoke about to the Lacedaemonians?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Oh! oh! oh! how stopped up I am! Whatever am I to do? It's not merely for the present that I am frightened; but when I have eaten, where is my crap to find an outlet now? This damned McPear fellow has bolted the door. Call a doctor; but who is the cleverest in this branch of the science? Amynon? Perhaps he would not come. Ah! Antisthenes! Let him be brought to me, cost what it will. To judge by his noisy sighs, that man knows what an arse wants, when it needs to crap. Oh! venerated Ilithyia! I shall burst unless the door gives way. Have pity! pity! Let me not become a thunder-mug for the comic poets.

div.stage: Enter Chremes, returning from the Assembly.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: Hi! friend, what are you doing there? You're not crapping, are you?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Oh! there! it is over and I can get up again.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: What's this? You have your wife's tunic on.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: It was the first thing that came to my hand in the darkness. But where are you coming from?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: From the Assembly.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Is it already over then?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: Certainly.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Why, it is scarcely daylight.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: I did laugh, ye gods, at the vermilion rope-marks that were to be seen all about the Assembly.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Did you get the triobolus?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: Would it had so pleased the gods! but I arrived just too late, and am quite ashamed of it; I bring back nothing but this empty wallet.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: But why is that?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: There was a crowd, such as has never been seen at the Pnyx, and the folk looked pale and wan, like so many shoemakers, so white were they in hue; both I and many another had to go without the triobolus.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Then if I went now, I should get nothing.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: No, certainly not, nor even had you gone at the second cock-crow.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Oh! what a misfortune! “Oh, Antilochus! no triobolus! Even death would be better! I am undone!” But what can have attracted such a crowd at that early hour?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: The Prytanes started the discussion of measures closely concerning the safety of the state; immediately, that blear-eyed fellow, the son of Neoclides, was the first to mount the platform. Then the folk shouted with their loudest voice, “What! he dares to speak, and that, too, when the safety of the state is concerned, and he a man who has not known how to save even his own eyebrows!” He, however, shouted louder than all of them, and looking at them asked, “Why, what ought I to have done?”

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Pound together garlic and laserpitium juice, add to this mixture some Laconian spurge, and rub it well into the eyelids at night. That's what I should have answered, had I been there.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: After him that clever rascal Evaeon began to speak; he was naked, so far as we all could see, but he declared he had a cloak; he propounded the most popular, the most democratic, doctrines. “You see,” he said, “I have the greatest need of sixteen drachmae, the cost of a new cloak, my health demands it; nevertheless I wish first to care for that of my fellow-citizens and of my country. If the fullers were to supply tunics to the indigent at the approach of winter, none would be exposed to pleurisy. Let him who has neither beds nor coverlets go to sleep at the tanners' after taking a bath; and if they shut the door in winter, let them be condemned to give him three goat-skins.”

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: By Dionysus, a fine, a very fine notion! Not a soul will vote against his proposal, especially if he adds that the flour-sellers must supply the poor with three measures of corn, or else suffer the severest penalties of the law; this is the only way Nausicydes can be of any use to us.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: Then we saw a handsome young man rush into the tribune, he was all pink and white like young Nicias, and he began to say that the direction of matters should be entrusted to the women; this the crowd of shoemakers began applauding with all their might, while the country-folk assailed him with groans.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And, indeed, they did well.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: But they were outnumbered, and the orator shouted louder than they, saying much good of the women and much ill of you.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And what did he say?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: First he said you were a rogue ...

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And you?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: Wait a minute! ... and a thief ...

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: I alone?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: And an informer.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: I alone?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: Why, no, by the gods! this whole crowd here.

div.stage: He points to the audience.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And who avers the contrary?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: He maintained that women were both clever and thrifty, that they never divulged the Mysteries of Demeter, while you and I go about babbling incessantly about whatever happens at the Senate.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: By Hermes, he was not lying!

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: Then he added that the women lend each other clothes, trinkets of gold and silver, drinking-cups, and not before witnesses too, but all by themselves, and that they return everything with exactitude without ever cheating each other; whereas, according to him, we are ever ready to deny the loans we have effected.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Yes, by Poseidon, and in spite of witnesses.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: Again, he said that women were not informers, nor did they bring lawsuits, nor hatch conspiracies; in short, he praised the women in every possible manner.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And what was decided?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: To confide the direction of affairs to them; it's the one and only innovation that has not yet been tried at Athens.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And it was voted?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And everything that used to be the men's concern has been given over to the women?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: You express it exactly.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Thus it will be my wife who will go to the courts now in my stead?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: And it will be she who will keep your children in your place.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: I shall no longer have to tire myself out with work from daybreak onwards?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: No, 'twill be the women's business, and you can stay at home and amuse yourself with farting the whole day through.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Well, what I fear for us fellows now is, that, holding the reins of government, they will forcibly compel us ...

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: To do what?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: ... to lay them.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: And if we are not able?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: They will give us no dinner.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: Well then, do your duty; dinner and love-making form a double enjoyment.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Ah! but I hate compulsion.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: But if it is for the public good, let us resign ourselves.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: It's an old saying that our absurdest and maddest decrees always somehow turn out for our good.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: May it be so in this case, oh gods, oh venerable Pallas! But I must be off; so, good-bye to you!

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Good-bye, Chremes. He goes back into his house.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.stage: Returning from the Assembly, still dressed like men; singing.
sp.p: March along, go forward. Is there some man following us? Turn round, examine everywhere and keep a good look-out; be on your guard against every trick, for they might spy on us from behind.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Let us make as much noise as possible as we tramp. It would be a disgrace for all of us if we allowed ourselves to be caught in this deed by the men. Come, wrap yourselves up well, and search both right and left, so that no mischance may happen to us. Let us hasten our steps; here we are close to the meeting-place whence we started for the Assembly, and here is the house of our leader, the author of this bold scheme, which is now decreed by all the citizens.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Let us not lose a moment in taking off our false beards, for we might be recognized and denounced. Let us stand under the shadow of this wall; let us glance round sharply with our eye to beware of surprises, while we quickly resume our ordinary dress. Ah! here is our leader, returning from the Assembly. Hasten to relieve your chins of these flowing manes. Look at your comrades yonder; they have already made themselves women again some while ago. They remove the beards as Praxagora and the other women enter from the right through the Orchestra.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Friends, success has crowned our plans. But off with these cloaks and these boots quick, before any man sees you; unbuckle the Laconian straps and get rid of your staffs;To the Leader. and you help them with their toilet. As for myself, I am going to slip quietly into the house and replace my husband's cloak and other gear where I took them from, before he can suspect anything.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: There! it's done according to your bidding. Now tell us how we can be of service to you, so that we may show you our obedience, for we have never seen a cleverer woman than you.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Wait! I only wish to use the power given me in accordance with your wishes; for, in the market-place, in the midst of the shouts and danger, I appreciated your indomitable courage.Just as she is about to enter the house Blepyrus appears in the doorway.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Eh, Praxagora! where are you coming from?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: How does that concern you, dear?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Why, greatly! what a silly question!

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: You don't think I have come from a lover's?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: No, perhaps not from only one.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: You can make yourself sure of that.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And how?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: You can see whether my hair smells of perfume.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: What? cannot a woman possibly be laid without perfume, eh!

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: The gods forfend, as far as I am concerned.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Why did you go off at early dawn with my cloak?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: A companion, a friend who was in labour, had sent to fetch me.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Could you not have told me?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Oh, my dear, would you have me caring nothing for a poor woman in that plight?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: A word would have been enough. There's something behind all this.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: No, I call the goddesses to witness! I went running off; the poor woman who summoned me begged me to come, whatever might betide.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And why did you not take your mantle? Instead of that, you carry off mine, you throw your dress upon the bed and you leave me as the dead are left, bar the chaplets and perfumes.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: It was cold, and I am frail and delicate; I took your cloak for greater warmth, leaving you thoroughly warm yourself beneath your coverlets.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And my shoes and staff, those too went off with you?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: I was afraid they might rob me of the cloak, and so, to look like a man, I put on your shoes and walked with a heavy tread and struck the stones with your staff.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: D'you know you have made us lose a sextary of wheat, which I should have bought with the triobolus of the Assembly?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Be comforted, for she had a boy.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Who? the Assembly?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: No, no, the woman I helped. But has the Assembly taken place then?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Did I not tell you of it yesterday?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: True; I remember now.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And don't you know the decrees that have been voted?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: No indeed.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Go to! you can live on lobster from now on, for they say the government is handed over to you.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: To do what —to spin?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: No, that you may rule ...

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: ... over all public business.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.stage: As she exclaims this Chremes reappears.
sp.p: Oh! by Aphrodite! how happy Athens will be!

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Why so?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: For a thousand reasons. None will dare now to do shameless deeds, to give false testimony or lay informations.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Stop! in the name of the gods! Do you want me to die of hunger?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: Good sir, let your wife speak.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: There will be no more thieves, nor envious people, no more rags nor misery, no more abuse and no more prosecutions and law-suits.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: By Poseidon! that's grand, if it's true!

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: I shall prove it and you shall be my witness and even he Pointing to Blepyrus. will have no objections to raise.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: You have served your friends, but now it behooves you to apply your ability and your care to the welfare of the people. Devote the fecundity of your mind to the public weal; adorn the citizens' lives with a thousand enjoyments and teach them to seize every favourable opportunity. Devise some ingenious method to secure the much-needed salvation of Athens; but let neither your acts nor your words recall anything of the past, for 'tis only innovations that please.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: But do not fail to put your plans into execution immediately; it's quick action that pleases the audience.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: I believe my ideas are good, but what I fear is that the public will cling to the old customs and refuse to accept my reforms.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Have no fear about that. Love of novelty and disdain for traditions, these are the dominating principles among us.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Let none contradict nor interrupt me until I have explained my plan. I want all to have a share of everything and all property to be in common; there will no longer be either rich or poor; no longer shall we see one man harvesting vast tracts of land, while another has not ground enough to be buried in, nor one man surround himself with a whole army of slaves, while another has not a single attendant; I intend that there shall only be one and the same condition of life for all.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: But how do you mean for all?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: You'll eat dung before I do!

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Won't the dung be common too?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: No, no, but you interrupted me too soon. This is what I was going to say: I shall begin by making land, money, everything that is private property, common to all. Then we shall live on this common wealth, which we shall take care to administer with wise thrift.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And how about the man who has no land, but only gold and silver coins, that cannot be seen?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: He must bring them to the common stock, and if he fails he will be a perjured man.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: That won't worry him much, for has he not gained them by perjury?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: But his riches will no longer be of any use to him.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: The poor will no longer be obliged to work; each will have all that he needs, bread, salt fish, cakes, tunics, wine, chaplets and chick-pease; of what advantage will it be to him not to contribute his share to the common wealth? What do you think of it?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: But is it not the biggest robbers that have all these things?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Yes, formerly, under the old order of things; but now that all goods are in common, what will he gain by not bringing his wealth into the general stock?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: If someone saw a pretty wench and wished to lay her, he would take some of his reserve store to make her a present and stay the night with her; this would not prevent him claiming his share of the common property.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: But he can sleep with her for nothing; I intend that women shall belong to all men in common, and each shall beget children by any man that wishes to have her.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: But all will go to the prettiest woman and try to lay her.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: The ugliest and the most flat-nosed will be side by side with the most charming, and to win the latter's favours, a man will first have to get into the former.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: But what about us oldsters? If we have to lay the old women first, how can we keep our tools from failing before we get into the Promised Land?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: They will make no resistance. Never fear; they will make no resistance.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Resistance to what?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: To the pleasure of the thing. This is the way that matters will be ordered for you.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: It's very well conceived for you women, for every wench's hole will be filled; but what about the men? The women will run away from the ugly ones and chase the good-looking.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: The ugly will follow the handsomest into the public places after supper and see to it that the law, which forbids the women to sleep with the big, handsome men before having satisfied the ugly shrimps, is complied with.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Thus ugly Lysicrates' nose will be as proud as the handsomest face?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Yes, by Apollo! this is a truly popular decree, and what a set-back it will be for one of those elegants with their fingers loaded with rings, when a man with heavy shoes says to him, “Give way to me and wait till I have done; you will pass in after me.”

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: But if we live in this fashion, how will each one know his children?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: The youngest will look upon the oldest as their fathers.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Ah! how heartily they will strangle all the old men, since even now, when each one knows his father, they make no bones about strangling him! then, my word! won't they just scorn and crap upon the old folks!

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: But those around will prevent it. Hitherto, when anyone saw an old man beaten, he would not meddle, because it did not concern him; but now each will fear the sufferer may be his own father and such violence will be stopped.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: What you say is not so silly after all; but it would be highly unpleasant were Epicurus and Leucolophas to come up and call me father.

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: But it would be far worse, were ...

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Were what?

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: ... Aristyllus to embrace you and style you his father.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: He'll regret it if he does!

sp.speaker: Chremes
sp.p: For you would smell vilely of mint if he kissed you. But he was born before the decree was carried, so that you have not to fear his kiss.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: It would be awful. But who will till the soil?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: The slaves. Your only cares will be to scent yourself, and to go and dine, when the shadow of the gnomon is ten feet long on the dial.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: But how shall we obtain clothing? Tell me that!

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: You will first wear out those you have, and then we women will weave you others.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Now another point: if the magistrates condemn a citizen to the payment of a fine, how is he going to do it? Out of the public funds? That would not be right surely.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: But there will be no more lawsuits.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: This rule will ruin you.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: I think so too. Besides, my dear, why should there be lawsuits?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Oh! for a thousand reasons, by Apollo! Firstly, because a debtor denies his obligation.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: But where will the lender get the money to lend, if all is in common? unless he steals it out of the treasury? and he could not hide that!

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Well thought out, by Demeter! But tell me this: here are some men who are returning from a feast and are drunk and they strike some passer-by; how are they going to pay the fine? Ah! you are puzzled now!

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: They will have to take it out of their pittance; and being thus punished through their belly, they will not care to begin again.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: There will be no more thieves then, eh?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Why steal, if you have a share of everything?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: People will not be robbed any more at night?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Not if you sleep at home. Even if you sleep outdoors there will be no more danger, for all will have the means of living. Besides, if anyone wanted to steal your cloak, you would give it to him yourself. Why not? You will only have to go to the common store and be given a better one.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: There will be no more playing at dice?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: What object will there be in playing?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: But what kind of life is it you propose to set up?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: The life in common. Athens will become nothing more than a single house, in which everything will belong to everyone; so that everybody will be able to go from one house to the other at pleasure.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And where will the meals be served?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: The law-courts and the porticoes will be turned into dining-halls.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And what will the speaker's platform be used for?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: I shall place the bowls and the ewers there; and young children will sing the glory of the brave from there, also the infamy of cowards,who out of very shame will no longer dare to come to the public meals.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Well thought out, by Apollo! And what will you do with the urns?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: I shall have them taken to the market-place, and standing close to the statue of Harmodius, I shall draw a lot for each citizen, which by its letter will show the place where he must go to dine. Thus, those for whom I have drawn an R will go to the royal portico if it's a T, they will go to the portico of Theseus; if it's an F, to that of the flour-market.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: To cram himself there like a capon?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: No, to dine there.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And the citizen whom the lot has not given a letter showing where he is to dine will be driven off by everyone?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: But that will not occur. Each man will have plenty; he will not leave the feast until he is well drunk, and then with a chaplet on his head and a torch in his hand; and then the women running to meet you in the crossroads will say, “This way, come to our house, you will find a beautiful young girl there.” —“And I,” another will call from her balcony, “have one so pretty and as white as milk; but before touching her, you must sleep with me.” And the ugly man, watching closely after the handsome fellows, will say, “Hi! friend, where are you running to? Go in, but you must do nothing; it's the ugly and the flat-nosed to whom the law gives the right to make love first; amuse yourself on the porch while you wait, in handling your fig-leaves and playing with yourself.” Well, tell me, does that picture suit you?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Marvellously well.

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: I must now go to the market-place to receive the property that is going to be placed in common and to choose a woman with a loud voice as my herald. I have all the cares of state on my shoulders, since the power has been entrusted to me. I must likewise go to busy myself about establishing the common meals, and you will attend your first banquet to-day.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Are we going to banquet?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: Why, undoubtedly! Furthermore, I propose abolishing the whores.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: And what for?

sp.speaker: Praxagora
sp.p: It's clear enough why; so that, instead of them, we may have the first-fruits of the young men. It is not meet that tricked-out slaves should rob free-born women of their pleasures. Let the courtesans be free to sleep with the slaves.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: I will march at your side, so that I may be seen and that everyone may say, “Look at the Dictator's husband!”

div.stage: He follows Praxagora into their house.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: As for me, I shall arrange my belongings and take inventory of them, in order that I may take them to the market-place.

div.stage: He departs.
There is an interlude of dancing by the Chorus, after which the man returns with his belongings and arranges them in a long line.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Come hither, my beautiful sieve, I have nothing more precious than you, come, all clotted with the flour of which I have poured so many sacks through you; you shall act the part of Canephorus in the procession of my chattels. Where is the sunshade carrier? Ah! this stew-pot shall take his place. Great gods, how black it is! it could not be more so if Lysicrates had boiled the drugs in it with which he dyes his hair. Hither, my beautiful mirror. And you, my tripod, bear this urn for me; you shall be the water-bearer; and you, cock, whose morning song has so often roused me in the middle of the night to send me hurrying to the Assembly, you shall be my flute-girl. Scaphephorus, do you take the large basin, place in it the honeycombs and twine the olive-branches over them, bring the tripods and the phial of perfume; as for the humble crowd of little pots, I will just leave them behind.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.stage: Watching First Man from a distance.
sp.p: What folly to carry one's goods to the common store; I have a little more sense than that. No, no, by Poseidon, I want first to ponder and calculate over the thing at leisure. I shall not be fool enough to strip myself of the fruits of my toil and thrift, if it is not for a very good reason; let us see first which way things turn. He walks over to Chremes. Hi! friend, what means this display of goods? Are you moving or are you going to pawn you stuff?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Neither.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Why then are you setting all these things out in line? Is it a procession that you are starting off to Hiero, the public crier?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: No, but in accordance with the new law that has been decreed, I am going to carry all these things to the market-place to make a gift of them to the state.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Oh! bah! you don't mean that.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Certainly.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Oh! Zeus the Deliverer! you unfortunate man!

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Why? It's as clear as noonday.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Must the laws not be obeyed then?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: What laws, your poor fellow?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Those that have been decreed.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Decreed! Are you mad, I ask you?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Am I mad?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Oh! this is the height of folly!

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Because I obey the law?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Is that the duty of a smart man?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Absolutely.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Say rather of a ninny.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Don't you propose taking what belongs to you to the common stock?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: I'll take good care I don't until I see what the majority are doing.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: There's but one opinion, namely, to contribute every single thing one has.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: I am waiting to see it, before I believe that.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: At least, so they say in every street.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: And they will go on saying so.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Everyone talks of contributing all he has.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: And will go on talking of it.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: You weary me with your doubts and dubitations.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Everybody else will doubt it.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: The pest seize you!

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: It will take you. Then seriously. What? give up your goods! Is there a man of sense who will do such a thing? Giving is not one of our customs. Receiving is another matter; it's the way of the gods themselves. Look at the position of their hands on their statues; when we ask a favour, they present their hands turned palm up so as not to give, but to receive.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Wretch, let me do what is right. Come, I'll make a bundle of all these things. Where is my strap?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Are you really going to carry them in?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Undoubtedly, and there are my two tripods strung together already.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: What folly! Not to wait to see what the others do, and then ...

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Well, and then what?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: ... wait and put it off again.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: What for?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: That an earthquake may come or an ill-omened flash of lightning, that a black cat may run across the street and no one carry in anything more, you fool!

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: It would be a fine thing if I were to find no room left for placing all this.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: You are much more likely to lose your stuff. As for placing it, you can be at ease, for there will be room enough as long as a month hence.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: I know these people; a decree is readily passed, but it is not so easily attended to.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: All will contribute their property, my friend.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: But what if they don't?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: But there is no doubt that they will.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: But anyhow, what if they don't?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Do not worry; they will.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: And what if they oppose it?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: We shall compel them to do so.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: And what if they prove the stronger?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: I shall leave my goods and go off.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: And what if they sell them for you?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: The plague take you!

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: And if it does?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: It will be a good riddance.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: You are really bent on contributing, then?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: 'Pon my soul, yes! Look, there are all my neighbors carrying in all they have.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Oh yes, it's Antisthenes; he's the type that would contribute! He would just as soon spend the next month sitting on the can.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: The pest seize you!

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Will Callimachus, the chorus-master, contribute anything?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Why, more than Callias!

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: The man must want to spend all his money!

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: How you weary me!

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Ah! I weary you? But, wretch, see what comes of decrees of this kind. Don't you remember the one reducing the price of salt?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Why, certainly I do.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: And do you remember that about the copper coinage?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Ah! that cursed money did me enough harm. I had sold my grapes and had my mouth stuffed with pieces of copper; indeed I was going to the market to buy flour, and was in the act of holding out my bag wide open, when the herald started shouting, “Let none in future accept pieces of copper; those of silver are alone current.”

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: And quite lately, were we not all swearing that the impost of one-fortieth, which Euripides had conceived, would bring five hundred talents to the state, and everyone was vaunting Euripides to the skies? But when the thing was looked at closely, it was seen that this fine decree was mere moonshine and would produce nothing, and you would have willingly burnt this very same Euripides alive.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: The cases are quite different, my good fellow. We were the rulers then, but now it's the women.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Whom, by Poseidon, I will never allow to piss on my nose.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: I don't know what the devil you're chattering about. Slave, pick up that bundle.

sp.speaker: Herald
sp.p: Let all citizens come, let them hasten at our leader's bidding! It is the new law. The lot will teach each citizen where he is to dine; the tables are already laid and loaded with the most exquisite dishes; the couches are covered with the softest of cushions; the wine and water are already being mixed in the ewers; the slaves are standing in a row and waiting to pour scent over the guests; the fish is being grilled, the hares are on the spit and the cakes are being kneaded, chaplets are being plaited and the fritters are frying; the youngest women are watching the pea-soup in the saucepans, and in the midst of them all stands Smoeus, dressed as a knight, washing the crockery. And Geron has come, dressed in a grand tunic and finely shod; he is joking with another young fellow and has already divested himself of his heavy shoes and his cloak. The pantry man is waiting, so come and use your jaws.

div.stage: Exit.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: All right, I'll go. Why should I delay, since the state commands me?

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: And where are you going to, since you have not deposited your belongings?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: To the feast.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: If the women have any wits, they will first insist on your depositing your goods.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: But I am going to deposit them.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: When?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: I am not the man to make delays.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: How do you mean?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: There will be many less eager than I.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: In the meantime you are going to dine.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: What else should I do? Every sensible man must give his help to the state.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: But if admission is forbidden you?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: I shall duck my head and slip in.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: And if the women have you beaten?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: I shall summon them.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: And if they laugh in your face?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: I shall stand near the door —

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: And then?

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: ... and seize upon the dishes as they pass.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: Then go there, but after me. Sicon and Parmeno, pick up all this baggage.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Come, I will help you carry it.

sp.speaker: First Man
sp.p: No, no, I should be afraid of your pretending to the leader that what I am depositing belonged to you.

div.stage: Exit with his belongings.

sp.speaker: Second Man
sp.p: Let me see! let me think of some good trick by which I can keep my goods and yet take my share of the common feast. He reflects for a moment. Ha! that's a fine idea! Quick! I'll go and dine, ha! ha!

div.stage: Exit laughing.
Interlude of dancing by the Chorus.
The scene shifts to a different section of Athens and the two houses are now to be thought of as those of two prostitutes.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.stage: Leaning out of the window of one house.
sp.p: How is this? no men are coming? And yet it must be fully time! Then it is for naught that I have painted myself with white lead, dressed myself in my beautiful yellow robe, and that I am here, frolicking and humming between my teeth to attract some passer-by! Oh, Muses, alight upon my lips, inspire me with some soft Ionian love-song!

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.stage: In the window of the other house.
sp.p: You putrid old thing, you have placed yourself at the window before me. You were expecting to strip my vines during my absence and to trap some man in your snares with your songs. If you sing, I shall follow suit; all this singing will weary the spectators, but is nevertheless very pleasant and very diverting.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.stage: Thumbing her nose at the Young Girl.
sp.p: Ha! here is an old man; take him and lead him away.To the flute-player.As for you, you young flute-player, let us hear some airs that are worthy of you and me.

Let him who wishes to taste pleasure come to my side. These young things know nothing about it; it's only the women of ripe age who understand the art of love, and no one could know how to fondle the lover who possessed me so well as myself; the young girls are all flightiness.

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.p: Don't be jealous of the young girls; voluptuousness resides in the pure outline of their beautiful limbs and blossoms on their rounded breasts; but you, old woman, you who are tricked out and perfumed as if for your own funeral, are an object of love only for grim Death himself.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: May your tongue be stopped; may you be unable to find your couch when you want to be loved. And on your couch, when your lips seek a lover, may you embrace only a viper!

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.p: Alas! alas! what is to become of me? There is no lover! I am left here alone; my mother has gone out. Interrupting her song. There's no need to mention the rest. Then singing again. Oh! my dear nurse, I adjure you to call Orthagoras, and may heaven bless you.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Ah! poor child, desire is consuming you like an Ionian woman; Interrupting again.and yet you are no stranger to the wanton arts of the Lesbian women.

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.p: But you shall not rob me of my pleasures; you will not be able to reduce or filch the time that first belongs to me.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Sing as much as you please, peep out like a cat lying in wait, but none shall pass through your door without first having been to see me.

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.p: If anyone enter your house, it will be to carry out your corpse. And that will be something new for you, you rotten old thing!

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Can anything be new to an old woman? My old age will not harm you.

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.p: Ah! shame on your painted cheeks!

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Why do you speak to me at all?

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.p: And why do you place yourself at the window?

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: I am singing to myself about my lover, Epigenes.

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.p: Can you have any other lover than that old fop Geres?

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Epigenes will show you that himself, for he is coming to me. See, here he is.

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.p: He's not thinking of you in the least.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Aye, but he is.

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.p: Old starveling! Let's see what he will do. I will leave my window.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: And I likewise. You will see I am much wiser than you.

sp.speaker: A Young Man
sp.p: Ah! could I but sleep with the young girl without first making love to the old flat-nose! It is intolerable for a free-born man.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Willy nilly, you must first gratify my desire. There shall be no nonsense about that, for my authority is the law and the law must be obeyed in a democracy.
But come, let me hide, to see what he's going to do.She retires.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Ah! ye gods, if I were to find the sweet child alone! the wine has fired my lust.

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.p: I have tricked that cursed old wretch; she has left her window, thinking I would stay at home. Ah! here is the lover we were talking of.

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.p: This way, my love, this way, come here and haste to rest the whole night in my arms. I worship your lovely curly hair; I am consumed with ardent desire. Oh! Eros, in thy mercy, compel him to my bed.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.stage: Standing beneath the Young Girl's window and singing.
sp.p: Come down and haste to open the door unless you want to see me fall dead with desire. Dearest treasure, I am burning to yield myself to voluptuous sport, lying on your bosom, to let my hands play with your bottom. Aphrodite, why dost thou fire me with such delight in her? Oh! Eros, I beseech thee, have mercy and make her share my couch.

sp.speaker: Young Woman
sp.p: Words cannot express the tortures I am suffering. Oh! my adored one, I adjure you, open your door for me and press me to your heart; 'tis for you that I am suffering.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Oh! my jewel, my idol, you child of Aphrodite, the confidante of the Muses, the sister of the Graces, you living picture of voluptuousness, oh! open for me, press me to your heart,'tis for you that I am suffering.He knocks.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: What are you knocking for? Are you looking for me?

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: What an idea!

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: But you were tapping at the door.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Death would be sweeter.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Why do you come with that torch in your hand?

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: I am looking for a man from Anaphlystia.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: What's his name?

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Oh! it's not Sebinus, whom no doubt you are expecting.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: By Aphrodite, you must, whether you like it or not.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: We are not now concerned with cases dated sixty years back; they are remanded for a later day; we are dealing only with those of less than twenty.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: That was under the old order of things, sweetheart, but now you must first busy yourself with us.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Aye, if I want to, according to the rules of draughts, where we may either take or leave.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: But it's not according to the rules of draughts that you take your seat at the banquet.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: I don't know what you mean; it's at this door I want to knock.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Not before knocking at mine first.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: For the moment I really have no need for old leather.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: I know that you love me; perhaps you are surprised to find me at the door. But come, let me kiss you.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: No, no, my dear, I am afraid of your lover.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Of whom?

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: The most gifted of painters.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: And who is he?

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: The artist who paints the little bottles on coffins. But get you indoors, lest he should find you at the door.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: I know what you want.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: I can say as much of you.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: By Aphrodite, who has granted me this good chance, I won't let you go.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: You are drivelling, you little old hag.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Rubbish! I am going to lead you to my couch.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: What need for buying hooks? I will let her down to the bottom of the well and pull up the buckets with her old carcass, for she's crooked enough for that.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: A truce to your jeering, poor boy, and follow me.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Nothing compels me to do so, unless you have paid the levy of five hundredths for me.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Look, by Aphrodite, there is nothing that delights me as much as sleeping with a lad of your years.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: And I abhor such as you, and I will never, never consent.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: But, by Zeus, here is something will force you to it.

div.stage: She shows him a document.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: A decree, which orders you to enter my house.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Read it out then, and let's hear.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Listen. “The women have decreed that if a young man desires a young girl, he can only lay her after having satisfied an old woman; and if he refuses and goes to seek the maiden, the old women are authorized to seize him and drag him in.”

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Alas! I shall become a Procrustes.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Obey the law.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: But if a fellow-citizen, a friend, came to pay my ransom?

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: No man may dispose of anything above a medimnus.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: But may I not enter an excuse?

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: There's no evasion.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: I shall declare myself a merchant and so escape service.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Beware what you do!

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Well! what is to be done?

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Follow me

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Is it absolutely necessary?

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Yes, as surely as if Diomedes had commanded it.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Well then, first spread out a layer of origanum upon four pieces of wood; bind fillets round your head, bring phials of scent and place a bowl filled with lustral water before your door.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Will you buy a chaplet for me too?

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Yes, if you outlast the tapers; for I expect to see you fall down dead as you go in.

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.p: Where are you dragging this unfortunate man to?

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: To my own bed.

sp.speaker: Young Girl
sp.p: That's not right. A young fellow like him is not of the age to suit you. You ought to be his mother rather than his wife. With these laws in force, the earth will be filled with Oedipuses.

div.stage: She takes him away with her.

sp.speaker: First Old Woman
sp.p: Oh! you cursed pest! it's envy that makes you say this; but I will be revenged.

div.stage: She goes back into her house.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: By Zeus the Deliverer, what a service you have done me, by freeing me of this old wretch! with what ardor I will show you my gratitude in a substantial form!

div.stage: Just as he begins to go in with the Young Girl an even older and uglier woman enters.

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: Hi! you there! where are you taking that young man to, in defiance of the law? The decree ordains that he must first sleep with me.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Oh! what a misfortune! Where does this hag come from? She's a more frightful monster than the other even.

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: Come here.

div.stage: She takes him by the arm.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Oh! I beg you, don't let me be led off by her!

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: It's not I but the law that leads you off.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: No, it's not the law, but an Empusa with a body covered with blemishes and blotches.

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: Follow me, my handsome little friend, come along quickly without any more ado.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Oh! let me go to the can first, so that I may gather my wits somewhat. Else I should be so terrified that you would see me letting out something yellow.

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: Never mind! you can crap, if you want, in my house.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: More than I want to, I'm afraid; but I offer you two good securities.

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: I don't require them.

div.stage: A Third Old Woman, the ugliest yet, now appears.

sp.speaker: Third Old Woman
sp.p: Hi! friend, where are you off to with that woman?

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: I am not going with her, but am being dragged by force. Oh! whoever you are, may heaven bless you for having had pity on me in my dire misfortune.Turns round and sees the Third Old Woman. Oh Heracles! oh Pan! oh Corybantes! oh Dioscuri! Why, she is still more awful! Oh! what a monster! great gods! Are you an ape plastered with white lead, or the ghost of some old hag returned from the dark borderlands of death?

div.stage: Taking his other arm.

sp.speaker: Third Old Woman
sp.p: No jesting! Follow me.

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: No, come this way.

sp.speaker: Third Old Woman
sp.p: I will never let you go.

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: Nor will I.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: But you will rend me asunder, you cursed wretches.

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: I'm the one he must go with according to the law.

sp.speaker: Third Old Woman
sp.p: Not if an uglier old woman than yourself appears.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: But if you kill me at the outset, how shall I afterwards go to find this beautiful girl of mine?

sp.speaker: Third Old Woman
sp.p: That's your problem. But begin by obeying.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Of which one must I rid myself first?

sp.speaker: Third Old Woman
sp.p: Don't you know? Come here.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Then let the other one release me.

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: Come to my house.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: If this dame will let me go.

sp.speaker: Third Old Woman
sp.p: No, by all the gods, I'll not let you go.

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: Nor will I.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: You would make very bad boatwomen.

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Because you would tear your passengers to pieces in dragging them on board.

sp.speaker: Third Old Woman
sp.p: Then come along, do, and hold your tongue.

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: No, by Zeus, come with me.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: It's clearly a case for the decree of Cannonus; I must cut myself in two in order to lay you both. But how am I to work two oars at once?

sp.speaker: Third Old Woman
sp.p: Easily enough; you have only to eat a full pot of onions.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Oh! great gods! here I am close to the door and being dragged in!

sp.speaker: Second Old Woman
sp.p: You will gain nothing by this, for I shall rush into your house with you.

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: Oh, no! no! better to suffer a single misfortune than two.

sp.speaker: Third Old Woman
sp.p: Ah! by Hecate, whether you wish it or not ...

sp.speaker: Young Man
sp.p: What a fate is mine, that I must make love to such a stinking harridan the whole night through and all day; then, when I am rid of her, I have still to tackle a brick-coloured hag! Am I not truly unfortunate? Ah! by Zeus the Deliverer; under what fatal star must I have been born, that I must sail in company with such monsters! But if my bark sinks in the sewer of these strumpets, may I be buried at the very threshold of the door; let this hag be stood upright on my grave, let her be coated alive with pitch and her legs covered with molten lead up to the ankles, and let her be set alight as a funeral lamp.The Young Man is dragged off by the two Old Women, one on each arm.

div.stage: Interlude of dancing by the Chorus.

sp.speaker: A Servant-Maid to Praxagora
sp.p: What happiness is the people's! what joy is mine, and above all that of my mistress! Happy are ye, who form choruses before our house! Happy are ye, both neighbors and fellow-citizens! Happy am I myself! I am but a servant, and yet I have poured on my hair the most exquisite essences. Let thanks be rendered to thee, Oh, Zeus! But a still more delicious aroma is that of the wine of Thasos; its sweet bouquet delights the drinker for a long time, whereas the others lose their bloom and vanish quickly. Therefore, long life to the wine-jars of Thasos! Pour yourselves out unmixed wine, it will cheer you the whole night through, if you choose the liquor that possesses most fragrance.To the Chorus.But tell me, friends, where is my mistress's husband?

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Wait for him here; he will no doubt pass this way.

sp.speaker: Maid-Servant
sp.p: Ah! there he is just going to dinner. Oh! master! what joy! what blessedness is yours!

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Mine?

sp.speaker: Maid-Servant
sp.p: None can compare his happiness to yours; you have reached its utmost height, you who, alone out of thirty thousand citizens have not yet dined.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Aye, here is undoubtedly a happy man.

sp.speaker: Maid-Servant
sp.p: Where are you off to?

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: I am going to dine.

sp.speaker: Maid-Servant
sp.p: By Aphrodite, you will be the last of all, far and away the last. Yet my mistress has bidden me take you and take with you these three young girls. Some Chian wine is left and lots of other good things. Therefore hurry, and invite likewise all the spectators whom we have pleased, and such of the judges as are not against us, to follow us; we will offer them everything they can desire.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: Generously invite everyone and omit no one, old or young. Dinner is ready for all; they need only go home. As for me, I shall go to the banquet with the customary torch in my hand.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: But why do you tarry, Blepyrus? Take these young girls with you and, while you are away a while, I will whet my appetite with some dining-song. I have but a few words to say:

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Let the wise judge me because of whatever is wise in this piece, and those who like a laugh by whatever has made them laugh. In this way I address pretty well everyone. If the lot has assigned my comedy to be played first of all, don't let that be a disadvantage to me; engrave in your memory all that shall have pleased you in it and judge the competitors equitably as you have bound yourselves by oath to do. Don't act like vile courtesans, who never remember any but their last lover.
It is time, friends, high time to go to the banquet - if we want to have our share of it - to go to the banquet. Open your ranks and let the Cretan rhythms regulate your dances.

sp.speaker: Blepyrus
sp.p: That's what I am doing.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: And you others, let your light steps too keep time.

Very soon we'll be eating lepadotemachoselachogaleokranioleipsanodrimypotrimmatosilphiotyromelitokatakechymenokichlepikossyphophattoperisteralektryonoptokephaliokinklopeleiolagoiosiraiobaphetragalopterygon. Come, quickly, seize hold of a plate, snatch up a cup, and let's run to secure a place at table. The rest will have their jaws at work by this time.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.stage: As they depart, dancing, with Blepyrus leading them.
sp.p: Dance gaily! Iai! Iai! We shall dine! Euoi! Euai! Euai! As for a triumph! Euoi! Euoi! Euai! Euai!
